name: DRY and the Wrong Abstraction
intent: Keep one authoritative place for each piece of knowledge, but do not merge code only because it looks alike: duplicated text that changes for different reasons is cheaper than an abstraction that fits neither.
scenario: A shop has two shipping-cost functions, one for retail orders and one for wholesale. Today they compute the same thing from the carrier's price list, so someone merges them into one function. During the year, change requests arrive: free shipping for big retail orders, a remote-area surcharge, a pallet discount and a fuel surcharge for wholesale, and every one of them concerns only one of the two cases.
problem: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) is often read as: never write the same lines twice. The real rule is about knowledge: every fact, such as a carrier tariff or a business rule, should have a single home, so a change is made once. But two functions can look alike because they happen to be the same today, not because they are the same fact. Merge them and each later difference becomes a flag and a branch, until the shared function serves nobody well and every change risks the other case.

howItWorks.title: Ask what changes together
howItWorks.text: The test for duplication is not whether lines match but why they would change. If the carrier raises its base price, both shipping functions must change at once: that is one piece of knowledge written twice. If retail gets free shipping, wholesale should not move: that is a coincidence of today's code, not shared knowledge. Merge the first kind, leave the second.

howItWorks.title: Watch what a merge turns into
howItWorks.text: A merged function starts clean. Then a change arrives for one case: add a boolean parameter and an if. Another arrives: one more flag. After four such changes the function has six parameters, and the flags can combine, so there are up to 2 to the power of the flag count paths to reason about. Callers must know which flags to set, and the function can no longer be understood without knowing both cases. Sandi Metz put it this way: duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

howItWorks.title: Wait for the pattern: the rule of three
howItWorks.text: A common habit is to tolerate the first copy, wince at the second, and abstract at the third. By then there are three real examples, so you can see what truly varies and what does not, instead of guessing from two. The number is a heuristic, not a law. What it protects you from is abstracting from too few cases.

howItWorks.title: Share the rule, keep the edges apart
howItWorks.text: When a true shared fact exists, extract just that: a tariff function that both shipping functions call. Each case keeps its own function for what is special to it. A carrier price change is then one edit, and a retail change cannot reach wholesale. The shared part is small and has a name that explains what it is.

howItWorks.title: Let YAGNI and KISS restrain DRY
howItWorks.text: YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it) says do not build something until it is needed: do not extract a general mechanism for a duplication that may never grow. KISS (keep it simple) says prefer the simplest thing that works, and two plain functions are often simpler than one clever one. DRY pushes towards one place for each fact; YAGNI and KISS push back against abstractions built early. They do pull against each other: following DRY alone creates the flag-filled function, following KISS alone leaves a tariff copied in five places.

pros: A fact that lives in one place is changed in one place, so copies cannot drift apart
Waiting for a third case means the abstraction is shaped by real differences
Sharing only the true rule keeps the shared code small and well named
Plain duplicated code is easy to read, delete and change independently
cons: Duplicated knowledge is real: the next change has to find every copy, and someone will miss one
Deciding whether two pieces change for the same reason takes judgement, and the answer is only certain in hindsight
Waiting for the rule of three means living with duplication longer than some teams like
An abstraction that is wrong is expensive to undo once other code has started to call it
whenToUse: Business rules, prices, limits and constants that appear in several places and must always agree
Schemas and configuration repeated across services or files, where a single source can generate the rest
Code that has already changed together several times, which is evidence of shared knowledge
whenNotToUse: Two pieces of code that look alike but belong to different features, teams or reasons to change
A first or second occurrence, when you cannot yet tell what will vary
A merge that needs a boolean parameter to say which of the two callers it is serving
pitfalls: Merging by looks: two functions with the same lines today but different owners, so the first divergent request adds a flag
Adding one more boolean to the shared function instead of splitting it, because deleting the abstraction feels like a step backwards: the sunk-cost trap
Treating the rule of three as a law, or as a reason to leave a copied business rule in two places for a year
Applying DRY to tests, so each test is a call into a helper full of parameters and none can be read alone
Hiding the real knowledge behind an abstraction that only works for today's two callers, so the third caller needs a workaround
Using YAGNI or KISS as an excuse to copy a tariff, a schema or a constant into many places: the restraint applies to speculative structure, not to a fact that is already repeated

quiz.question: Two functions have identical bodies today, but one belongs to the billing team and the other to the reporting team. What does DRY, read as a rule about knowledge, suggest?
options: Merge them at once, because identical lines are always the same piece of knowledge.
Merge them behind a flag, so each team can still choose its own behaviour later.
Move both into a shared library, so the code lives in one place with a clear owner.
Leave them apart unless they must change together: they may be the same text but not the same fact.
quiz.explanation: DRY is about one authoritative home for each fact, not about identical text. Two owners with their own reasons to change are a warning sign: merging couples them, and a flag only postpones the damage.

quiz.question: A merged shipping function has gained four boolean flags, one per request. A fifth request concerns only wholesale. What is usually the best next step?
options: Add a fifth flag, because the function already exists and all callers use it.
Move the new rule into a subclass of the function's caller, to avoid editing the function.
Inline the function back into each caller, then keep only the truly shared part.
Wait for a sixth request, so that the rule of three can show what to do.
quiz.explanation: When an abstraction no longer fits, the cheap fix is to inline it into its callers and let each drop what it does not need, then extract only the part that is really shared. Adding flags is the sunk-cost trap. The rule of three guards against abstracting too early, not against undoing it.

quiz.question: A tariff constant of 500 cents is written in five different services. Someone says YAGNI and KISS mean it should stay copied. Why is that a misuse?
options: The constant is one fact repeated five times, so DRY applies, and YAGNI limits speculative structure only.
KISS never applies to constants, since a constant is not code that can be made complex.
YAGNI forbids duplication of any kind, so the copies would have to go in any case.
A constant can only be shared safely if it is first wrapped in an interface and a factory.
quiz.explanation: YAGNI and KISS restrain abstractions built for needs that may never come. A repeated business fact is already real, and one missed copy is a bug. Extracting a named constant is the simplest thing that works. The principles pull against each other, and judgement decides which one wins.
